problem:
Given the linear transformation $T:[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}3x-8y \\ 16y-6x\end{aligned}],$
find  $2\cdot \text{nullity}(T)-3.$

activity_context.topic_title: The Kernel of a Linear Transformation

examples.knowledge_point: Finding the Nullity of a Linear Transformation
examples.worked_solution:
First, we write down the standard matrix of $\mathbf{T}\mathbin{:}$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14071281/assets/f27d3195556ff8786f9416cddbe4ad52cf1838f2b0ce37b4da11746fee59fb9c.png)

Recall that $\textrm{nullity}(\mathbf{T}) = \textrm{nullity}(T) = \textrm{dim}(\textrm{Null}(T)).$

In order to find $\textrm{dim}(\textrm{Null}(T)),$ we reduce $T$ to row echelon form, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}T & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 4 & 0 \\ 4 & 10 & -1 \\ -6 & -12 & 1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-2){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}2 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & -1 \\ -6 & -12 & 1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+3{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}2 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has no non-pivot columns. Therefore, 

$$
\textrm{nullity}(\mathbf{T})=\textrm{dim}(\textrm{Null}(T))=0.
$$

feedback.problem: Find a basis of $\,\text{Ker}(T)$ given that $T:[\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}3y-6z-6x \\ -4y+x+z \\ 2y+8z+8x\end{aligned}].$
feedback.worked_solution:
Finding the kernel of $\,T\,$ is equivalent to finding the null space of the standard matrix of $\,T.$

For the given linear transformation, the standard matrix is $T=[\begin{aligned}-6 & 3 & -6 \\ 1 & -4 & 1 \\ 8 & 2 & 8\end{aligned}].$

Setting $x=[\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}],$ we then need to solve the equation $Tx=0.$ First, we reduce $T$ to row echelon form, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}T & =[\begin{aligned}-6 & 3 & -6 \\ 1 & -4 & 1 \\ 8 & 2 & 8\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+\frac{1}{6}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-6 & 3 & -6 \\ 0 & -\frac{7}{2} & 0 \\ 8 & 2 & 8\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+\frac{4}{3}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-6 & 3 & -6 \\ 0 & -\frac{7}{2} & 0 \\ 0 & 6 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+\frac{12}{7}{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-6 & 3 & -6 \\ 0 & -\frac{7}{2} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The basic variables are the variables whose coefficients are pivots. In this case, the basic variable is $x$ and $y$, and we have one free variable, $z.$ That means we need to find $x$ and $y$ in terms of $z.$

From the second equation, we get $y=0.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we have $x=-z.$ 

Therefore, if $x\in \text{Ker}(T),$ then 

$$
x=[\begin{aligned}-z \\ 0 \\ z\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]z,\,z\in R.
$$

This implies that $B={[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]}$ is a basis of $\text{Ker}(T).$
